n: In this lecture we will consider the analysis of antidepressants, diuretics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; the outline also includes the topic of nitrogen-containing synthetic drugs. Key terms: furosemide, ethacrynic acid, indomethacin, ibuprofen, ketotifen. In the DVSSM set, the key terms also include fluoxetine, venlafaxine, mirtazapine, amitriptyline and acetazolamide.

Definition of antidepressants and their generations. Antidepressants treat depression: mood improves, and sleep and appetite are normalised. The first generation is tricyclic: imipramine was synthesised in 1957, and amitriptyline appeared later. The second generation is heterocyclic; it includes trazodone, mianserin and maprotiline. The third generation is the selective inhibitors, of which fluoxetine is an example.

Clinical classification of antidepressants. The sedative group is used in depressive agitation: trimipramine, doxepin, amitriptyline, azafen and others. The stimulant group is used in apathetic states: imipramine, desipramine, nortriptyline, fluoxetine. The balanced group is used in both cases: maprotiline, tianeptine, sertraline, venlafaxine. That is, the choice depends on the clinical condition of the patient.

Toxicological significance of antidepressants. In poisoning, dizziness, headache, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth and blurred vision are observed. Skin rashes, euphoria and insomnia appear. Hallucinations and mental disturbances also occur.

Metabolism of antidepressants. They are rapidly metabolised in the liver: N-demethylation, hydroxylation and conjugation with glucuronic acid occur. 60-70 % of the drug is excreted in the urine as metabolites. About 5-10 % is excreted in the urine unchanged. This means that in analysis the metabolites must also be sought.

Choosing the sample and isolation. In screening analyses urine is usually taken. In severe poisoning or in the case of death, little of the substance may be found in urine, so analysis of blood is important. Liquid-liquid and solid-phase extraction are used for isolation. The sample is extracted in an alkaline medium with a solvent such as n-hexane; the organic layer is re-extracted into an acidic solution and determined by HPLC or GC.

Fluoxetine. Fluoxetine, known as Depres, Prozac and under other names, is an antidepressant with basic properties; molecular mass 345.8 (309.3). It is a white crystalline powder: soluble in methanol at 250 mg/ml, in chloroform at 125 mg/ml, and also soluble in ethanol and acetone; sparingly soluble in water, maximum 14 g/l, at 25 °C. Insoluble in benzene, toluene, cyclohexane and hexane. Melting point 157.5-158.7 °C.

Data sheet for fluoxetine and venlafaxine. Fluoxetine, Latin name Depresum, is an antidepressant with basic properties; molecular mass 345.8 (309.3). The formula of venlafaxine is C17H27NO2, molecular mass 277.4; it is also an antidepressant with basic properties. Synonyms of venlafaxine: Dobupal, Efexor, Effexor, Trevilor, Trewilor and Vandral.

Venlafaxine and the TOXI-TUBES method. Venlafaxine is an antidepressant with basic properties, formula C17H27NO2, molecular mass 277.4. The procedure: 5 ml of urine or 2.5 ml of blood and 2.5 ml of water are placed in a TOXI-TUBES-A tube and shaken for 5 minutes. The emulsion is centrifuged at 3000 rpm. The organic layer is dried, the residue is dissolved in 1 ml of alcohol and analysed by TLC.

TLC systems. For paroxetine, benzene, dioxane and 25 % ammonia in the ratio 60:35:5 or ethanol and 25 % ammonia 100:1.5 are used. For fluoxetine, that is, Depres, alcohol, chloroform and benzene 2:1:2; for venlafaxine ethyl acetate, alcohol and NH3 8.5:1:0.5. For mirtazapine the system ethyl acetate, methanol, water and NH3 is used. As the visualising reagent, UV light and Dragendorff's and Mandelin's reagents are used.

GC and HPLC methods. Gas chromatography is widely used to determine tricyclic antidepressants, with capillary columns; the disadvantage is that derivatisation with trifluoroacetic anhydride is necessary. In HPLC, C8 and C18 sorbent is used, with a perchlorate-based mobile phase or one impregnated with methylamine; UV detector 254 nm, mobile phase acetonitrile and methanol. From blood it is possible to isolate trimipramine, doxepin, amitriptyline, imipramine, desmethyldoxepin, nortriptyline and desipramine.

Mirtazapine. The formula of mirtazapine is C17H19N3, molecular mass 265.3; known as Remeron, Zispin and under other names. A white crystalline powder, sparingly soluble in water, soluble in methyl alcohol and chloroform; it melts at 114-116 °C. In the UV spectrum a solution in 96 % ethyl alcohol has high absorption at λ=295 nm. In TLC the system ethyl acetate, methanol, water and 25 % ammonium hydroxide 87:3:1.5:0.5 is used; with Dragendorff a brown spot, Rf=0.42.

Action and significance of amitriptyline. Amitriptyline is an anticholinergically active substance: dry mouth, pupil dilation and urinary retention are observed; in alcoholic psychoses up to 200-300 mg is recommended. It is significant both as a drug used in medicine and because toxicomaniacs consume it as an intoxicating substance. It potentiates the effect of narcotic, psychotropic and hypnotic substances and prolongs the duration of action. Symptoms: drowsiness, dizziness, unsteady gait, twitching of the muscles of the hands, allergy and cardiac rhythm disturbance. The drug is produced as tablets and ampoules: amitriptyline, triptisol.

t: Isolating amitriptyline from blood and urine
n: Isolating amitriptyline from blood and urine. To 5 ml of blood or 50 ml of urine, 30 % NaOH is added, pH=9-10, then it is extracted twice with 20 ml of ether. The ether isolates are transferred into a 50 ml volumetric flask and made up to the mark with ether. The isolate is distributed into 4 vessels in portions of 10, 10, 10 and 20 ml and evaporated to dryness.

Amitriptyline: colour and crystal reactions. Concentrated H2SO4, Marquis and Fröhde reagents give a candy-coloured tint; this is for amitriptyline and nortriptyline. With Mandelin's reagent a brown, then green colour forms. With Reinecke's salt, amitriptyline forms needle-like crystals, sensitivity 0.02 µg; nortriptyline forms branched crystals, 0.01 µg.

Amitriptyline: two-stage TLC. The isolate is applied to the plate as a spot and a streak; as the witness solution the bases of amitriptyline and nortriptyline are spotted. First system: benzene - acetone 80:20, 10 cm; second: benzene - dioxane - 25 % ammonia 60:35:5, another 10 cm; then concentrated H2SO4. Amitriptyline Rf=0.74-0.78, candy-coloured spot; nortriptyline Rf=0.38-0.46, yellow; the detection limit is 0.2 µg. If there is no spot at Rf=0.74-0.78, the conclusion is that amitriptyline is absent.

Amitriptyline: UV, IR and quantification. In the UV spectrum in 0.1 % HCl solution there is high absorption at 197, 202, 207 and 240 nm. IR spectrum: 756, 746, 770, 969, 1014, 1258 cm⁻¹. The amount is determined by photoelectrocolorimetric and UV spectrophotometric methods.

Imipramine, that is, imizine. The first tricyclic antidepressant, imipramine, was synthesised in 1957; it belongs to the stimulant group. It is anticholinergically active and is used in diseases with depressive experiences; with frequent use, insomnia may occur. Metabolism: deamination, dealkylation, hydrolysis and conjugation; the metabolites are excreted in the urine. With concentrated HNO3 it gives a blue colour, then dull green, brown; with picric acid, a yellow precipitate. UV, in 0.01 M HCl, in the range 220-350 nm max 251 nm.

Classification of diuretic drugs. Groups: xanthine derivatives; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, for example acetazolamide, and osmotic diuretics. The thiazide group, hydrochlorothiazide; furosemide and ethacrynic acid. Potassium-sparing diuretics: spironolactone and triamterene.

Toxicological significance of diuretics. A fall in blood pressure, tachycardia, collapse, arrhythmia and aplastic anaemia are observed. Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperglycaemia, raised cholesterol and gout occur. Loss of appetite, dry mouth, intense thirst, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and pancreatitis appear. Dizziness, drowsiness, muscle relaxation, disturbances of hearing and vision, and allergic reactions may also occur.

t: Isolating diuretics by the aqueous acetone method
n: Isolating diuretics by the aqueous acetone method. The biological object is infused with an acetone - water 5:3 mixture, then saturated with sodium chloride. The acetone is distilled off; the aqueous layer is extracted with ethyl acetate under acidic and alkaline conditions. The alkaline layer is re-extracted with chloroform. The organic layers are purified by TLC.

Identifying furosemide. An alcoholic solution of furosemide, under the action of p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde, forms a green compound that turns dark red. In the azo dye reaction, hydrolysis with 1 mol/l HCl is carried out first; then sodium nitrite, ammonium sulphamate and N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine hydrochloride are added, and a red-violet colour forms. Ammonium sulphamate is added to destroy the excess sodium nitrite in the solution.

Hydrochlorothiazide: reactions and TLC. Under the action of cobalt chloride a light-blue precipitate forms, and under the action of copper(II) sulphate a green-blue precipitate. TLC systems: chloroform - benzene - 2-propanol 2:4:1 and chloroform - ethyl acetate - 2-propanol 10:5:1. Visualising reagents: for hydrochlorothiazide mercury(II) sulphate and diphenylcarbazide; for furosemide FeCl3; for acetazolamide Dragendorff, according to Munier; for ethacrynic acid 0.5 % KMnO4.

UV spectra of diuretics. Furosemide absorbs in alcohol at 274 nm; its metabolite 4-chloro-5-sulfamoylanthranilic acid at 267 nm. Hydrochlorothiazide in alcohol at 272 nm, acetazolamide in alcohol at 264 nm. Ethacrynic acid gives a maximum in alcohol at 278 nm.

NSAIDs, that is, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: maximum daily doses. The maximum daily doses of the drugs differ. Ibuprofen 2400 mg, naproxen 1250 mg, indomethacin 200 mg. Piroxicam 30 mg, diclofenac sodium 150 mg, ketoprofen 3000 mg.

NSAIDs: dangerous effects and doses. NSAIDs accumulate in the kidneys and disrupt their function; even in a short time the function of the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys and liver is impaired. Signs: severe abdominal pain, bloody vomiting, gastric ulcer, raised blood pressure, risk of bleeding, renal failure and allergy. Maximum daily doses: ibuprofen 2400 mg, naproxen 1250 mg, indomethacin 200 mg, piroxicam 30 mg, diclofenac sodium 150 mg, ketoprofen 3000 mg. In self-poisoning with a large amount of ibuprofen, death occurred from cardiovascular failure and perforation of a gastric ulcer.

Diclofenac and ibuprofen. Diclofenac sodium is a phenylacetic acid derivative, melting point 283-285 °C; in the retard form 100 mg gives 0.5 µg/ml in the blood after 4 hours; 99 % is bound to albumins. 50 % of diclofenac is metabolised in the liver, 60 % is excreted by the kidneys; half-life 1-2 hours. Ibuprofen is a white crystalline powder, melting point 75-77 °C; practically insoluble in water; peak in the blood at 1-2 hours; half-life 1.8-2.5 hours.

Indomethacin, ketoprofen and piroxicam. The melting point of indomethacin is 155-162 °C, polymorphism exists; practically insoluble in water; peak in the blood at 1-2 hours, in the retard form 2-4 hours; T½ 4-5 hours. Food slows the absorption of indomethacin; as suppositories it is absorbed less. The melting point of ketoprofen is 93-96 °C, and that of piroxicam 198-200 °C.

NSAIDs: colour reactions and TLC. With Liebermann's reagent diclofenac gives a reddish-brown colour, indomethacin dark grey, ibuprofen orange, ketoprofen brown, piroxicam reddish-yellow. In TLC chloroform and methanol 9:1 are used, the visualising reagent being Marquis. Rf values: diclofenac 0.47, indomethacin 0.38, ibuprofen 0.54, ketoprofen 0.57, piroxicam 0.48. In the UV spectrum, in 96 % alcohol, diclofenac 272 and 275 nm, indomethacin 278 nm, ibuprofen 257, 263, 272 nm.

Sulphonylurea derivatives, that is, SUDs. Among antidiabetic agents, sulphonylurea derivatives are widely used and are a cause of poisoning. Isolation is carried out by the aqueous acetone method; extractant: for glibenclamide chloroform, for gliquidone benzene, for glipizide n-heptane, for gliclazide and glimepiride ethyl acetate. In TLC chloroform - acetone 9:1. HPLC retention times: glipizide 8.45, gliclazide 9.97, glibenclamide 11.73, glimepiride 12.47, gliquidone 14.58 minutes.

SUDs: visualising reagents and TLC. To identify SUDs in TLC the solvent system chloroform-acetone 9:1 is used. For gliquidone a 1 % solution of cobalt nitrate in ethanol is used, for gliclazide a 10 % solution of phosphomolybdic acid in methanol. For glibenclamide Liebermann's reagent; for all except glimepiride Marquis reagent.

SUDs: HPLC and UV indicators. In HPLC a Zorbax Eclipse XDB C18 column, 150×4.6 mm, 5 µm, flow rate 0.8 ml/min, 40 °C, detector 210 nm. Retention times, in minutes: glipizide 8.45, gliclazide 9.97, glibenclamide 11.73, glimepiride 12.47, gliquidone 14.58. UV spectrum in alcohol: glibenclamide 275 and 300 nm, gliquidone 311 nm, gliclazide 263 and 274 nm, glipizide 275 nm, glimepiride 274 nm.

t: The essence of the TDSIS method
n: The essence of the TDSIS method. Thermodesorption surface-ionisation spectroscopy, TDSIS, is a new method with high sensitivity that makes it possible to determine very small amounts of a substance. It makes it possible to determine and analyse residues of nitrogen-containing, poorly volatile, physiologically active compounds. Nano-amounts can be analysed with an accuracy of 1·10⁻¹¹ g without chromatographic separation. The essence: molecules are evaporated in a temperature-programmed mode and recorded in the surface-ionisation detector as a thermodesorption spectrum.

t: TDSIS: detector and stages of analysis
n: TDSIS: detector and stages of analysis. The anode of the detector is a heated emitter, and the cathode is a collector of positive ions. Qualitative analysis is carried out from the effective desorption temperatures and by comparison with the reference spectrum, that is, a data bank. Stages: preparing the indicator, sample solution, application to the evaporator tape, TDSIS analysis and comparison with the reference.

TDSIS analysis conditions. The emitter consists of oxidised molybdenum with an iridium alloy; emitter voltage 405 V; emitter temperature 390-420 °C. Evaporation temperature from room temperature to 505 °C; air flow 50 l/hour, compressor voltage 12 V. The sample volume taken for analysis is 1.0 µl.

Stages of TDSIS analysis. The analysis proceeds in several stages. First the indicator and sample solutions are prepared. The sample solution is applied to the PII-N-S “Iskovich-1” evaporator tape and the TDSIS analysis is carried out. The thermodesorption spectra are stored in the data bank, compared with the reference spectrum, and the result is interpreted.

The general scheme of analysis. First stage: isolation from blood or urine with an organic solvent in an alkaline medium; for diuretics the aqueous acetone method is used. For confirmation, colour and crystal reactions, TLC with visualising reagents, and UV and IR spectra are used. The amount is determined by photoelectrocolorimetry, UV spectrophotometry, GC and HPLC; the TDSIS method gives a sensitive analysis without separation.

Conclusion. Antidepressants, that is, amitriptyline, imipramine, fluoxetine and others, are metabolised in the liver; 5-10 % is excreted in the urine unchanged. Amitriptyline in TLC Rf=0.74-0.78, nortriptyline Rf=0.38-0.46; diuretics are isolated by the aqueous acetone method. TDSIS determines the molecules of a substance in nano-doses without separation. NSAIDs, in turn, are dangerous to the kidneys and the gastrointestinal tract.
